n: The same day as the conflict in chapter 12, Jesus leaves the house and sits by the Sea of Galilee — the setting for his great sermon in parables.
The crowd is so large that Jesus teaches from a boat just offshore. Teachers usually sat to teach, and the water helped carry his voice.

f.w: he went into a ship, and sat

n: Jesus begins teaching in parables — stories from everyday life with a deeper spiritual meaning. The first is about a farmer sowing seed.

f.g: Greek parabolē — “to throw alongside”: a comparison that sets a familiar story beside a spiritual truth.

f.w: a sower went forth to sow

n: Farmers scattered seed by hand, so some landed on the hard, trampled path where birds quickly ate it.

f.g: fowls = birds.

n: Some fell on rocky ground with only a thin layer of soil. Those seeds sprouted quickly because the shallow soil warmed fast.

f.g: Limestone bedrock lying just under a thin layer of soil — common in Galilee.
forthwith = immediately.

n: But with no deep roots, the young plants withered in the hot sun.
Other seed fell among thorn roots. The thorns grew up with the grain and choked it out.

f.g: Thistles and weeds whose roots were already in the soil.

n: Some seed fell on good soil and produced an amazing harvest — thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was sown.
A call to listen closely. A parable rewards those who think about it and want to understand.
The disciples ask why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables instead of speaking plainly.

f.w: Why speakest thou unto them in parables?

n: The disciples have been given to understand the “mysteries” of the kingdom — truths revealed to the faithful, not hidden secrets of a club.

f.g: Greek mystērion — truths knowable only by revelation.

n: A spiritual law: those who receive and use truth are given more; those who reject it lose even what they had.

f.w: whosoever hath, to him shall be given

f.g: The JST reads “whosoever continueth not to receive.”

n: Parables reveal truth to seekers but conceal it from those who have closed their minds. They look without truly seeing.
Jesus applies Isaiah’s prophecy about people who hear God’s word but won’t understand it.

f.w: By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand

n: The problem lies in the heart. People have grown dull and shut their eyes, so they don’t turn to God and receive healing.

f.g: waxed = grown, become; gross = thick, dull, insensitive.
converted = turned around, turned back to God.

n: The disciples are blessed because they are willing to see and hear.
Ancient prophets longed to witness the Messiah’s coming. The disciples are living it.

f.w: many prophets and righteous men have desired to see

n: Now Jesus privately explains the parable of the sower.
The path stands for those who hear but don’t understand. Satan quickly snatches the word away before it can take root.

f.g: Satan.

n: Rocky ground is the person who receives the word with instant joy — an enthusiastic but shallow start.

f.g: anon = immediately.

n: Without deep roots, that faith lasts only until trials come. Then the person stumbles and falls away.

f.g: dureth = endures, lasts.
by and by = soon, immediately.

n: Thorny ground pictures people whose worries and love of money crowd out the word until it bears no fruit.
Good ground is the person who hears, understands, and bears fruit. The harvest varies, but all are fruitful.
A new parable: the kingdom is like a farmer who plants good seed in his field.
At night an enemy secretly sows weeds among the wheat. Such sabotage was a known act of revenge in the ancient world.

f.g: Probably darnel, a poisonous weed that looks almost identical to wheat in its early growth.

n: Only when the grain begins to form does the difference become clear.

f.g: The green stalk.

n: Puzzled servants ask the owner how weeds got into a field sown with good seed.

f.g: The owner and master of the estate.

n: The owner knows an enemy did it. The servants offer to pull the weeds right away.
He says no. The roots are tangled, and pulling the weeds now would destroy the good wheat as well.

f.w: lest while ye gather up the tares

n: Both will grow until harvest, then be separated. Latter-day revelation and the JST reverse the order: the wheat is gathered first, then the tares burned.

f.w: Gather ye together first the tares
f.g: The JST reads “gather ye together first the wheat into my barn; and the tares are bound in bundles to be burned.”

n: The kingdom is like a mustard seed — tiny at the start, but it grows remarkably large.
The proverbially smallest seed becomes a large shrub where birds can nest. Christ’s kingdom begins small and grows to shelter many.

f.g: Garden plants.

n: A little yeast hidden in a large batch of dough silently works through the whole thing. The gospel quietly transforms people and the world.

f.g: Yeast or a bit of fermented dough used to make bread rise.
Roughly 40 liters of flour — enough bread to feed over a hundred people.

n: To the crowds Jesus now taught only in parables.

f.w: without a parable spake he not unto them

n: Matthew sees this as fulfilling a psalm in which the speaker opens his mouth in parables to reveal ancient truths.

f.w: I will open my mouth in parables
from the foundation of the world

n: In the house, away from the crowd, the disciples ask Jesus to explain the parable of the wheat and tares.

f.g: Explain to us.

n: The sower of good seed is Jesus himself, the Son of Man.
The field is the whole world. The good seed are people who belong to God’s kingdom; the weeds are those who follow the evil one.
The devil sowed the weeds; the harvest is the end of the age; the reapers are angels.

f.g: The JST adds “or the destruction of the wicked.” Greek aiōn means age or era.

n: As weeds are gathered and burned, so will it be at the end of this age.
Angels will remove from Christ’s kingdom everything that causes sin and all who do evil.

f.g: Everything that causes people to stumble into sin.

n: Their fate is pictured as a blazing furnace — a symbol of the anguish of the wicked.
The righteous will shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom — a beautiful image of glory.
A man stumbles on buried treasure, hides it again, and joyfully sells everything to buy the field. The kingdom is worth all we have.

f.g: With no banks, people often buried valuables in the ground for safekeeping.

n: A second picture of the same truth: a merchant actively searching for fine pearls.

f.g: goodly = fine, beautiful.

n: Finding one pearl of exceptional worth, he sells everything to buy it. The kingdom of God is worth any sacrifice.

f.g: The Pearl of Great Price, one of the Latter-day Saint standard works, takes its name from this parable.

n: The kingdom is like a dragnet pulled through the sea that catches all kinds of fish.

f.g: A dragnet, weighted at the bottom and floated at the top, drawn between boats or to shore.

n: Fishermen sort the catch, keeping the good and throwing out the bad (including fish forbidden under the law).
Like the wheat and tares, this pictures a final separation of the wicked from the righteous at the end of the age.

f.w: sever the wicked from among the just

f.g: sever = separate.

n: Jesus repeats the solemn warning about the furnace and the weeping of the lost.
Jesus checks for understanding. The disciples say yes.

f.w: Have ye understood all these things?
f.g: Understanding is the mark of “good ground” (v. 23).

n: A disciple trained in the kingdom is like a homeowner bringing out both new and old treasures — combining ancient scripture with Christ’s new revelation.
Having finished these parables, Jesus moves on — Matthew’s marker for the end of a major discourse.

f.w: when Jesus had finished these parables

n: Back in his hometown of Nazareth, Jesus teaches in the synagogue. People are amazed but puzzled about where he got such wisdom and power.

f.g: His hometown, Nazareth.

n: They know him as the carpenter’s son and know his whole family. Familiarity makes it hard to see him as anything more.

f.g: Greek tektōn — a builder who might work in wood or stone.

f.w: James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas
f.g: Jesus’s younger half-brothers; James and Judas (Jude) are traditionally linked to the epistles of James and Jude.

n: His sisters live there too. They think they know exactly who he is, so his greatness offends them.
They take offense. Jesus observes that prophets are honored everywhere except at home, where people think they know them best.

f.w: A prophet is not without honour

n: Because of their unbelief, Jesus did few miracles there. Miracles follow faith; they don’t force it.
